newsitem.title: USA: Gold supply/demand tightly balanced in 1997 - CPM.
newsitem.headline: Gold supply/demand tightly balanced in 1997 - CPM.

text.p: Gold supply and fabrication demand remain tightly balanced in 1996, a situation which should persist next year, New York based CPM Group said in its "Gold Survey 1996" published Tuesday.
"This year the flow of newly refined gold coming onto the market could reach 89.0 million ounces, up 4.2 percent from 1995," CPM Group research director Joseph Rosta said.
"In 1997 supply is projected at 91.0 million ounces, a 2.2 percent increase."
South African mine production continues to slide in 1996 though, Rosta said.
South African gold output could fall 5.3 percent this year to 15.9 million ounces and could fall a further 0.6 percent in 1997 to 15.8 million.
"Improvement in work rules and regulations should lead to more stable production for several years in South Africa, perhaps at the 16.0 million ounce level," he said.
But rising mine production in Canada, the U.S., Australia and other developed economies is more than offsetting the lower levels of South African production.
Meanwhile, the recovery of refined gold from recycled scrap is projected at 17.0 million ounces annually in 1996 and 1997, representing a 17.2 percent rise from 1995.
Exports from former Soviet Union countries could trend higher next year, possibly reaching 12 million ounces, CPM said.

On the demand side, gold use in jewelry and other manufactured products is projected at 96.8 million ounces in 1996, up 5.3 percent from 91.9 million ounces in 1995. Demand could reach 97.1 million ounces in 1997, the research company forecasts.
Demand from the jewelry sector is seen rising at a more moderate pace, next year, possibly expanding 0.6 percent to 89.5 million ounces.
At the same time, electronics use could be flat, while demand from dental alloyers and other manufacturers may post a significant decline.
